conservation.notes: Least Concern. Common and widespread in scrub, dry farmland and around human habitation across sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East and South Asia, and established in Western Australia after introduction to Perth in 1889. It is a resident breeder almost everywhere it occurs, so there is no migration to or from the modelled regions.

human_tolerance.notes: At home in dry farmland, cultivation and the edges of human habitation, and 'often becoming very tame'; it feeds on the ground in fields, savanna and gardens without needing to be fed. It is a dry-scrub and farmland specialist rather than a city bird, so it is placed as an Adapter rather than an Exploiter, and it roosts communally in low bushes and trees by day.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: Southern African window; the article's nearest dated statement is 'mainly May to November in Zimbabwe'. The same article describes the African breeding season as spread out and almost year-round in Malawi, so this is a window on a resident, multi-brooded breeder, not a single season.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: Egyptian window, from 'February to June in Egypt and Tunisia'. Phase dates are a judgement placed around the described months.

inat.skipped: ISO 3166-2 region given without --inat-place-id; pass --inat-place-id <id> (look it up at https://www.inaturalist.org/places) to query iNaturalist for this subdivision

vocalizations.description: Low rolling chuckling call, 'croo-doo-doo-doo-doo', with a rising and falling amplitude, described as more musical than the coo of other doves. Given year-round, above all by the male following the female in courtship with head-bobbing, and by a pair calling to one another.

taxonomy.note: GBIF backbone gives Spilopelia senegalensis (Linnaeus, 1766) as ACCEPTED, with Columba senegalensis Linnaeus, 1766 as its basionym; the parentheses around the authority follow the schema's own example. ITIS searchByScientificName returns TSN 1125211 for the same binomial with the same authority.

external.note: GBIF usageKey 6101223 and iNaturalist taxon id 1455922 are the identifiers the issue's data pointers cite; Wikidata Q391198 carries P846 (GBIF) 6101223 and P3151 (iNaturalist) 1455922, and P815 (ITIS TSN) 1125211, which agrees with the ITIS web service. ebird_code 'laudove' is the eBird species code for Spilopelia senegalensis, taken from the eBird/Clements taxonomy code used by the Birds of the World import.

common_names.note: Wikidata labels for Q391198: en 'Laughing Dove', fr 'Tourterelle maillée' (frwiki Tourterelle maillée), de 'Palmtaube' (dewiki Palmtaube), nl 'Palmtortel' (nlwiki Palmtortel). Each language's sitelink sits on a species article covering the same taxon.

conservation.note: IUCN category LC is the status shown in the English Wikipedia infobox (from BirdLife International's 2018 assessment e.T22690445A132060894); Wikidata P141 (IUCN conservation status) is Least Concern. The remaining note text is the article's own distribution and habitat summary plus the Perth introduction. The IUCN Red List page itself is not openly licensed and was not used as a source.

range.note: The article gives no country list, so this list is a judgement mapping of the five subspecies ranges it does give onto ISO 3166-1 codes. S. s. phoenicophila 'Morocco to northwest Libya' -> MA, DZ, LY. S. s. aegyptiaca 'Nile Valley (Egypt)' -> EG. S. s. senegalensis 'west Arabia, Socotra Island, Africa south of the Sahara' -> SA, YE plus the Sahelian, East and southern African countries of the dry and semi-desert belt, from Senegal east to Somalia and south to South Africa (the central African rainforest states are left out, as this is a dry-habitat species). S. s. cambayensis 'east Arabia and east Iran to Pakistan, India and Bangladesh' -> the Gulf states (OM, QA, KW, BH, AE), IR, PK, IN, BD. S. s. ermanni 'Kazakhstan, north Afghanistan, west China' -> KZ, AF, CN; the distribution paragraph's 'Kyrgyzstan' adds KG. The African part is a resolution of 'much of Sub-Saharan Africa', so the list is representative rather than exhaustive. introduced = AU (the nominate population was introduced to Perth in 1889 and is established around Perth and Fremantle) and ES (the Spanish article records an established feral population). Deliberately left out of both lists: TR, SY, LB, IL, PS, JO, CY, GR and AE, which the distribution paragraph says are 'also found' in but adds 'these populations may be derived from human introductions' - the same article's subspecies list contradicts itself about the Arabian populations, so those codes are left unclaimed rather than guessed. mdd_id and ncbi_taxon_id are omitted: no openly licensed source for them was confirmed here.

traits.limb_count.note: A bird: two legs plus wings, and the schema counts walking limbs only.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: 'They are fairly terrestrial, foraging on the ground in grasslands and cultivation' and 'Their flight is quick and direct with the regular beats and an occasional sharp flick of the wings'. Doves walk (with the familiar head-bob) rather than hop, so Hop is omitted; the described glide in the courtship display is folded into Fly, since the schema separates only powered flight and gliding as distinct gaits and a single flight animation has to cover both.

traits.flight.note: 'Their flight is quick and direct with the regular beats and an occasional sharp flick of the wings characteristic of pigeons in general' - powered flight.

traits.nest_type.note: 'The nest is a very flimsy platform of twigs built in a low bush and sometimes in crevices or under the eaves of houses' - Platform is the dominant type; the crevice/eave sites are treated under shelter_tag and the nest_platform resource.

traits.perching.note: 'Small numbers assemble on trees near waterholes before flying to the water's edge'; the nest is built in a low bush.

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg (0.082 kg, far below 1 kg).

traits.mass_kg.note: AVONET (AVONET1_BirdLife sheet) gives Mass = 82.13 g for Spilopelia senegalensis, with Mass.Source = 'Dunning' (the CRC Handbook of Avian Body Masses), Inference = 'NO' (measured, not imputed), and n = 9 individuals. Converted to 0.082 kg. The AVONET measurement is retained without claiming that it matches other reported mass ranges.

traits.length_m.note: The English article gives 'typically 25 cm (9.8 in) in length'; the French article gives 'environ 27 centimètres' with a tail of 10.5-12 cm. The English figure is used because it is the one stated as typical.

traits.lifespan_y.note: Judgement, and an honest gap. No open-licensed source with a lifespan figure for Spilopelia senegalensis was found: English Wikipedia gives none, Wikidata carries no longevity property for Q391198, and the published life-expectancy figures (a mark-recapture study at Barberspan, South Africa, W. R. J. Dean 1977 in Ostrich; Avibase; a Western Australian ringing study) all sit behind licences this repository rejects, so they were not used. 3 years is a judgement for a small resident African dove, in the range this repository already sources for other small birds (Erithacus rubecula 1.1 y, Troglodytes troglodytes 2.0 y, Turdus merula 2.4 y) and well below the maximum ages reported for the species in those non-open sources.

traits.diet.note: 'Laughing doves eat the fallen seeds, mainly of grasses, other vegetable matter and small ground insects such as termites and beetles'; AVONET gives Trophic.Level Herbivore and Trophic.Niche Granivore. Grasses and fallen seeds are mapped to 'seed'; 'other vegetable matter' (soft green plant matter) to 'browse', the closest non-seed plant category; termites and beetles to 'invertebrate'. The shares are a rounded judgement - 'mainly' seeds, a small insect supplement - not a measured diet.

traits.social.note: 'The species is usually seen in pairs or small parties and only rarely in larger groups. Larger groups are formed especially when drinking at waterholes in arid regions.' structure = Pair; group_size = [2, 12] is a judgement spanning a pair and a small party, since the sources give no numbers.

traits.activity_pattern.note: All described activity - ground foraging, courtship, flocking at waterholes, roosting in low bushes - is by day; no nocturnal activity is described, and AVONET records Migration = 1 (resident).

traits.defense.note: 'Their flight is quick and direct' and nesting adults 'may feign injury to distract and draw predators away from the nest'; the primary response to a threat (the lizard buzzard and southern grey shrike are named as its predators) is to flush and fly off, so Flee rather than Freeze or Mob.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement. 'A common and widespread species in scrub, dry farmland, and in areas of human habitation, often becoming very tame' puts it lower than a typical wild bird, but it is a ground-foraging dove that flushes readily and it is not the tame, food-seeking commensal a feral pigeon is, so it is set mid-range rather than near zero.

habitat.use.note: 'They are fairly terrestrial, foraging on the ground in grasslands and cultivation' (AVONET Primary.Lifestyle = Terrestrial), with birds 'assemble on trees near waterholes' and nesting in low bushes; the remainder is flight. A judgement split of ground/arboreal/aerial, not a sourced fraction.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: Birds roost and loaf in low bushes and trees ('small numbers assemble on trees near waterholes', nests 'built in a low bush'), so 'perch' is the closest ResourceTag; the crevices and eaves sometimes used for nesting have no dedicated tag.

habitat.resources.note: seed/browse/invertebrate weights follow the diet shares above (seed weighted highest); nest_platform weight reflects the flimsy twig platform, which may be built in a bush, a crevice or under eaves; perch weight reflects communal roosting in bushes and trees; shrub_thicket reflects the low-bush nest and roost; water reflects 'small numbers assemble on trees near waterholes before flying to the water's edge where they are able to suck up water'. All qualitative, not measured.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: urban_affinity, uses_gardens and the note follow the described dry-farmland, cultivation and near-inhabitation lifestyle, and the fact that this is a dry-scrub specialist rather than a city bird, which is why it is an Adapter and not an Exploiter. light_max, flight_distance_m and the roosting remark are judgement; the sources give no measured light tolerance or flight-initiation distance.

seasonal.strategy.note: 'It is a resident breeder' and 'They are mostly sedentary but some populations may make movements'; AVONET Migration = 1. Local movements (Gujarat-ringed birds recovered 200 km north in Pakistan) are not a migration.

seasonal.phases.note: 'The species has a spread out breeding season in Africa. Almost year-round in Malawi and Turkey; and mainly May to November in Zimbabwe, February to June in Egypt and Tunisia. In Australia the main breeding season is September to November.' The two phases above are windows taken from the Zimbabwe (used as the southern African proxy for ZA) and Egypt statements; start/end dates are a judgement placed around the described months.

seasonal.life_stages.note: 'The eggs hatch after about 13 to 15 days' (midpoint 14 used for Egg duration_days) and 'the young fledge and leave the nest after about 14 to 16 days' (midpoint 15 used for Juvenile duration_days). The juvenile scale is a judgement approximation of a partly feathered squab on leaving the nest.

activity.note: Curves generated by tools/fetch_activity.py, one run per region; the per-region sources, methods, observation counts and query URLs are recorded in activity.regions[].

vocalizations.coo.note: The chuckling call is a low rolling croo-doo-doo-doo-doo with rising and falling amplitude, described as more musical than the call of most doves. It is given year-round, chiefly by males following females in courtship displays and by pairs calling to one another. Mapped to Song, the closest available context for this display and pair-bonding call; no alarm context is inferred from it.

look.note: Plumage follows the nominate African form: pinkish-brown underside with lilac-tinged head and neck, buff lower abdomen, brown upperparts, a bluish-grey wing band, white-tipped graduated tail, red legs, and an adult rufous-and-grey checker patch on each side of the neck; young birds lack the neck marks. Proportions are judgement, guided by the description 'long-tailed, slim pigeon', the French article's 10.5-12 cm tail against about 27 cm total length, AVONET's 17.8 mm culmen, and 18.9 mm tarsus. The narrow body and raised head are species-specific look judgements (girth_ratio 0.7 and neck_angle_deg 30) that expose the head/neck junction in the shared biped_winged plan, which has no separate neck part. Two accent tiles on each lateral side sit over the rufous head colour to suggest the grey-and-rufous checker patch; this places the mark on the sides, not the nape. The five-slot palette cannot represent a dark iris and red legs separately, so the eye slot carries the documented leg red and the iris uses the dark markings slot. Subspecies vary in shade, including paler arid-zone populations, which this one model does not represent.

behavior.note: A species-specific copy of the shared perching-songbird tree preserves perching, nesting, singing and flight responses while using walk for ground-feeding, consistent with this record's Walk locomotion mode. Its threat response flees without emitting the courtship coo as an alarm, since no separate alarm call is sourced. The local defaults use seed for food and coo for song. flee_m = 6 is judgement; nest building is limited explicitly to May-November, matching the Zimbabwe breeding window.
